title: Approval Matrix Setup for Multi-Entity P2P: Why One-by-One Configuration Fails and How to Fix It
summary: Configuring approval matrices user by user breaks P2P governance. Learn how role-based approval groups and email approvals fix multi-entity setups.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Approval matrices that are configured one approver at a time break down as soon as a group runs several entities and a few hundred users, because every resignation, promotion or new subsidiary needs manual edits. Moving to role-based approval groups, a single group-wide policy template, SSO-linked access, delegation and one-click email or chat approvals turns the matrix into a maintained control. Most multi-entity groups can migrate in one 12 to 16 week deployment cycle per batch of markets.


## Why Approval Matrix Setup Becomes the Hardest Part of P2P


Ask a regional finance team what slows down their procure-to-pay process and the answer is rarely invoice volume. It is approvals. Not the act of approving, but keeping the rules about who approves what correct.


This came through clearly in a recent discovery conversation Peakflo held with the finance team of a regional manufacturing and distribution group running five subsidiaries across Southeast Asia. They were replacing an older approval system. Their reason was simple: the current tool had no straightforward approval matrix configuration. Every rule had to be set up one by one, which made it manual and time-consuming. With a few hundred users spread across Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam and Indonesia, each change in staff or structure meant hours of rework.


Their priority list for the replacement told the same story: approvals reviewable from email, OCR, better reporting, two- and three-way matching, a full audit trail, and above all a simple approval matrix setup. The P2P process came first because, in their words, it was the most complicated and most important process they had for controlling expense approvals and governance.


That pattern is common. A[Gartner finance research](https://www.gartner.com/en/finance) theme over recent years is that control quality depends on whether policy is enforced inside the workflow rather than documented beside it. An approval matrix that lives in a spreadsheet and is copied manually into a system is documented, not enforced.


This guide covers why one-by-one approval configuration fails, what a maintainable approval matrix looks like, and how to migrate a multi-entity group without disrupting payments. If you are designing payment authorisation tiers specifically, see our companion piece on[manufacturing payment approval matrix design](https://peakflo.co/blog/manufacturing-payment-approval-matrix-multi-currency-ai) . This article focuses on the setup and upkeep problem across the full P2P chain.


## What Is an Approval Matrix?


An approval matrix is the set of rules that decides who must approve a document before it moves to the next stage. In P2P, that covers four objects:


1. **Purchase requests (PRs)** , approved by the budget owner and sometimes procurement
2. **Purchase orders (POs)** , approved before the order is sent to the supplier
3. **Supplier invoices or bills** , approved when there is an exception or no PO
4. **Payments** , approved by authorisers under maker-checker rules


Each rule combines conditions such as entity, amount, currency, cost centre, category and vendor with an approver or chain of approvers. The matrix is the main way finance applies[segregation of duties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_duties) and the authorisation principles described in the[COSO internal control framework](https://www.coso.org/guidance-on-ic) .


## Why One-by-One Approval Configuration Fails


### Every staff change becomes a configuration project


When rules point at named people, a single resignation can touch dozens of rules across entities. A promotion means removing someone from one tier and adding them to another. With a few hundred users, staff movement alone can generate weekly maintenance.


### Rules drift apart between entities


Teams that configure each entity separately end up with five slightly different matrices. Thailand might need two approvals above a threshold while Malaysia needs three, not because of policy but because someone set them up differently a year ago. Regional finance loses the ability to state the group policy with confidence.


### Leavers stay in approval chains


If the approval system has its own logins, leavers keep access until someone remembers to remove them. Documents also route to inboxes nobody reads. Both are audit findings waiting to happen.


### Approvers are forced to log in for every decision


Older tools often require approvers to open the application, find the document and approve inside it. Busy country heads approve in batches once a week, and suppliers wait.


### Nobody can see which rule fired


When an auditor asks why a PO for a given amount was approved by one person and not two, the team has to reconstruct the logic from screenshots and emails.


The table below summarises the operational impact.


Symptom Root cause Business impact


Approvals routed to leavers Rules point at named users, no SSO Stuck documents, late payments, audit findings


Different rules per country Each entity configured separately Inconsistent governance, policy cannot be stated clearly


Hours of rework after reorganisations No designations or approval groups Finance analysts spend days on maintenance


Slow approvals from senior staff Approval requires login to the tool Longer PR-to-PO and invoice cycle times


Weak audit evidence No record of which rule applied Longer audits and more sample testing


## What a Maintainable Approval Matrix Looks Like


A maintainable matrix has five properties. Each one removes a category of manual work.


### 1. Rules point at roles, not people


Instead of naming a person, each rule points at a designation or approval group: Budget Owner, Country Finance Manager, Finance Director SEA, VP APAC. The system resolves whoever currently holds that role. When the person changes, only the role assignment changes. Peakflo calls these approval groups, and routing follows whoever is tagged to the designation at the time the document is submitted.


### 2. One group-wide policy template


The group defines its policy once: which documents need approval, the amount bands, which conditions trigger extra levels. Entities inherit the template, with local thresholds expressed in their own currency. A purchase in Vietnamese dong and one in Singapore dollars follow the same logic.


### 3. Access tied to corporate identity


[Single sign-on](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/enterprise-apps/what-is-single-sign-on) through Microsoft Entra ID (Outlook) or Google Workspace means a leaver loses access to the approval system the day their email is disabled. Only user creation needs a bulk upload. Offboarding happens automatically.


### 4. Delegation for every approval group


Approvers set out-of-office delegations with a start and end date, and pending documents reroute to the backup. Our guide to[approval delegation and fallback approvers](https://peakflo.co/blog/approval-delegation-fallback-approvers-finance-workflows) covers how to design backup chains in detail.


### 5. Approvals happen where approvers already are


Approvers receive one consolidated daily email listing every document awaiting them, with configurable fields so they can decide without opening the tool. They can approve with one click, from mobile, or inside Microsoft Teams or Slack. Comments and @mentions back to the requester land in the audit trail.


The next table compares the two models across the full lifecycle.


Capability One-by-one configuration Role-based approval matrix


Rule target Named user Designation or approval group


New entity setup Rebuild rules from scratch Inherit group template, set local thresholds


Leaver handling Manual removal from each rule and tool Automatic via SSO and role reassignment


Approver experience Log in to approve One-click email, mobile, Teams or Slack


Leave cover Ad hoc forwarding Dated delegation rules


Audit evidence Screenshots and emails Timestamped trail of rule, approver and comments


Maintenance effort Hours per change Minutes per change


## Designing the Approval Matrix: A Practical Template


Below is an illustrative structure for a five-entity group. Thresholds are examples only and should be set by your finance policy.


Document Condition Level 1 Level 2 Level 3


Purchase request Any amount Budget Owner Country Head above band A Finance Director SEA above band B


Purchase order Converted from approved PR Procurement Country Finance Manager above band A VP APAC above band C


PO-backed invoice Matched within tolerance Auto-approve None None


PO-backed invoice Exception outside tolerance Requester Country Finance Manager None


Non-PO invoice Any amount Cost Centre Owner Country Finance Manager above band A Finance Director SEA above band B


Payment batch Any amount Maker (AP) Checker (Finance Manager) Authoriser above band C


A few design rules keep the matrix lean:


- Keep it to two to four levels. Each extra level adds delay without proportionate control.
- Let matched invoices auto-approve. If the PO was approved and the invoice matches it within tolerance, a second approval is duplication. Our article on[approval workflow bottlenecks from manual routing](https://peakflo.co/blog/approval-workflow-bottlenecks-manual-routing) explains how much time this saves.
- Express amount bands in local currency per entity, and review them annually against FX movement.
- Use category or vendor conditions for risk, for example IT purchases always go to IT, capital items always go to finance.


## How to Migrate from a Legacy Approval System


Migration is where most projects stall, because the existing matrix is rarely documented. A six-step approach works for most groups.


1. **Export and audit current rules.** List every live rule by entity, document and threshold. Flag rules pointing at leavers and duplicated approvers.
2. **Define designations and approval groups.** Replace names with roles. Agree who holds each role in each entity.
3. **Build one policy template.** Agree amount bands and conditions at group level, then set local currency values.
4. **Connect SSO and set delegation.** Link access to the corporate identity provider and set backups for every group.
5. **Enable approvals in email and chat.** Choose the fields each approver sees so they can decide without logging in.
6. **Test in UAT, then go live by market batch.** Run real documents through each rule, sign off, train users by role, then cut over.


For a group with five entities, sequencing matters. The team in the discovery call above planned to go live in Malaysia and Singapore first, because those two markets produced the most invoice and payment requests, even though Thailand had the most staff. Starting where transaction volume is highest proves the matrix under real load. We cover sequencing in more depth in our guide to[phased multi-country P2P rollout](https://peakflo.co/blog/multi-country-p2p-rollout-strategy-southeast-asia-phased-implementation) .


## Measuring Whether the New Matrix Works


Track these indicators before and after go-live:


Metric What it tells you Typical direction after migration


PR-to-PO cycle time Speed of front-end approvals Falls as approvers act from email


Documents pending more than 3 days Approval bottlenecks Falls with delegation and reminders


Rule changes per month Maintenance load Falls as rules point at roles


Approvals by leavers or wrong role Control failures Should reach zero with SSO


Audit sample exceptions Evidence quality Falls with timestamped trails


[McKinsey’s operations research](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/operations/our-insights) on procurement digitisation repeatedly points to cycle-time and compliance metrics as the earliest visible gains. Approval metrics are usually the first to move.

## Our Verdict: Is It Time to Rebuild Your Approval Matrix?


After reviewing how multi-entity groups manage approvals, here is our recommendation.


### Rebuild now if


- Your current tool needs each approver configured individually
- You run three or more entities with different local rules
- Staff changes regularly cause stuck documents
- Approvers must log in to approve
- Auditors ask for evidence you assemble manually


### You can wait if


- You run a single entity with fewer than 30 approvers
- Your approval rules have not changed in a year and nobody has left
- Your ERP already enforces role-based routing with SSO


**Our Recommendation:** If the matrix is the reason you are replacing your current tool, treat it as the core design artefact of the project. Agree roles and a group template first, then pick software that routes by role, ties access to SSO and lets approvers act from email. Groups that do this typically cut matrix maintenance from hours per change to minutes and remove approval-related audit findings within the first cycle.


## Conclusion


An approval matrix is only as strong as its upkeep. Configuring approvers one by one works for a single office. It does not work for five countries, hundreds of users and a regional VP who needs to trust that the policy is applied the same way everywhere.


Role-based approval groups, a shared template, SSO, delegation and approvals in email or chat solve the upkeep problem at its root. Combined with[two-way and three-way matching](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/two-way-three-way-matching) so that matched invoices do not need a second sign-off, they turn approvals from a bottleneck into a control that largely runs itself.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is an approval matrix in procure-to-pay?


An approval matrix is the rulebook that decides who must approve a purchase request, purchase order, invoice or payment, based on conditions such as entity, amount, cost centre, category and vendor. In P2P it is the main control that stops unauthorised spend.


### Why does configuring approvals one by one cause problems?


When each approver is hard-coded user by user, every reorganisation, resignation or new entity forces manual edits across dozens of rules. Rules drift apart between entities, approvers get missed, and nobody can confirm which version of the matrix is live.


### What is the difference between user-based and role-based approval routing?


User-based routing points each rule at a named person. Role-based routing points rules at a designation or approval group such as Finance Director SEA, and the system resolves whoever currently holds that role. Role-based routing survives staff changes without rule edits.


### Can approvers approve purchase requests without logging in?


Yes. Modern approval workflow software sends a consolidated email with the key fields of each document and a one-click approve button. Approvals can also be actioned from mobile, Microsoft Teams or Slack, while the audit trail still records who approved and when.


### How many approval levels should a multi-entity P2P matrix have?


Most groups use two to four levels: budget owner, department or country head, finance, and a regional executive above a high threshold. More levels add delay without adding much control, so thresholds should push only high-value or high-risk spend to the top tiers.


### How does SSO help maintain an approval matrix?


Single sign-on through Microsoft Entra ID or Google Workspace ties P2P access to the corporate email account. When an employee leaves and their email is disabled, they automatically lose access to the approval system, so leavers cannot sit in an approval chain.


### What happens to approvals when an approver goes on leave?


Delegation rules route pending approvals to a named backup for a defined start and end date. Without delegation, documents wait in the inbox of someone who is away, which is one of the most common causes of late supplier payments.


### Should each entity have its own approval matrix?


Each entity should share one group-wide policy template, with local differences limited to thresholds, currencies and local approvers. A shared template keeps governance consistent across countries while allowing for local currency values and statutory requirements.


### How long does it take to migrate from a legacy approval system?


For a group with a few entities and a few hundred users, a typical migration runs in a 12 to 16 week deployment cycle covering design, configuration, user acceptance testing, training, cutover and go-live, usually with markets batched together.


### What should an approval matrix template include?


A good template lists the document type, entity, amount bands in local currency, cost centre or category conditions, the approval group for each level, delegation backups, escalation timing and the audit evidence required. It should be maintained in the system, not in a spreadsheet.
